rule: bad: this rule can never fire — the participle "boiled in sea-water" becomes an invented boiling event inside the condition that no actual boiling can ever match, so mire-essence is never derived from it. Rewrite as "When silken threads are boiled in sea-water, the threads yield mire-essence.": a finite condition clause with an explicit subject, the shape your first two texts already use successfully.
texts: good. fires once per boiling, with the Keepers, the threads, the sea-water, the forming and the cauldron all covered.
good. the same fireable shape, with the cauldron as the yielder and the yielding tied back to the boiling.
good. a plain fact — the Keepers, the taking, the sea-water and the named tide-pools as its source are all recorded, and both names are kept.
good. denies the yielding at the level of the two kinds, and "fresh water" is kept as water that is fresh.
